summary:
Yalova is a province of Turkey and stands under Turkey's national framework on gender identity and sexual orientation. No trans-specific statute, enforcement pattern, police practice or incident documentation specific to Yalova appears in the available sources. That gap is recorded as absence of documented divergence rather than evidence of local permissiveness: the national rules and the national enforcement climate apply in Yalova as they apply across Turkey.

The national enforcement climate a visitor enters is documented in Kaos GL's 2025 review, “The Year of the Family: A Major Siege Against LGBTI+ People,” which finds hostility toward LGBTI+ people has become explicit state policy. Instructions framed around “the Year of the Family” were issued to public institutions, an LGBTI+ rights organisation was closed for the first time in years, expression and artistic freedom were restricted, and events were cancelled or banned.

The same review records 6 right-to-life violations over the year, including 3 hate-motivated killings, with trans people the most affected; 89 torture or ill-treatment violations, up from 51 the prior year; 313 liberty violations, about two and a half times the previous year, of which 299 were detention decisions; private-life violations rising from 16 to 67, among them obstruction of trans people's hormone therapy; and 61 travel bans.
tangentialFactors:
The 2025 counts are national totals for Turkey as a whole, not figures attributable to Yalova; they indicate the enforcement environment a trans visitor in Yalova stands under, not a measured local rate.

The obstruction of hormone therapy recorded among private-life violations bears directly on a trans visitor who needs medication during a stay, since hormone replacement therapy is not covered by the government healthcare system and must be obtained and paid for privately.
localsOnly:
For trans residents of Yalova, the closure of an LGBTI+ rights organisation, the cancellation or banning of events, and the “Year of the Family” instructions to public institutions shape the local civic space, as does the national pattern of 299 detention decisions and 61 travel bans recorded in 2025.

Residents seeking legal recourse face the national position that Turkey has no comprehensive law prohibiting discrimination on sexual orientation or gender identity, and no direct discrimination protection for gender identity.
outOfScopeNotes:
No Yalova-specific source was available in this inventory; the province-level characterisation rests on the absence of local documentation rather than on a Yalova field survey, and remains unresolved whether undocumented local practice diverges from the national pattern.

Whether the draft legislative package reported before the government in October 2025 has since passed is unresolved in the sources.
blindSummary:
The country has no visa, entry or border rule specific to LGBTQ travellers, and the documented exposure points lie inside the country rather than at the frontier. The visitor-facing document risk is general: foreigners must carry original photo ID at transit checkpoints in holiday destinations, with fines of up to 3,000 Turkish lira and warnings of detention for non-compliance. For a trans visitor, that requirement intersects with identity checks on the street: in August 2025 police in the largest city stopped roughly 20 trans women while they were walking, shopping or sitting in cafés, held them at a central police station and released them after ‘General Information Gathering’ background checks. Legal experts quoted in the domestic press argue those checks breach Article 5 of a regional human-rights convention. One detainee's account captures the practical position: nothing was fined, but names and details were recorded, and officers were already applying a regime that had not been enacted.

Criminalisation by statute had not been enacted when a major international rights organisation reported on 29 October 2025, but a draft legislative package then before the government would effectively criminalise LGBT people under vague provisions protecting 'the family' and 'public morals'. The sitting government has repeatedly used that framing to legitimise stigmatisation, and the reform sits within a broader authoritarian drift. Whether the package has since passed is unresolved in the sources.

A national LGBTI+ human rights report records 313 violations over 2025, roughly two and a half times the 2024 total, dominated by 299 detention decisions — 256 taken on the record and 43 off it — alongside systematic attacks on the privacy of LGBT people. Domestic press coverage of the same report counts six deaths linked to anti-LGBTQ violence in 2025, three classified as hate killings, with transgender individuals disproportionately affected. Hostility of this scale is best read as state policy rather than residual prejudice.

Policing asymmetry is documented at the level of individual cases. In August 2024 a trans woman was knifed in a district of the largest city by a 17-year-old; the attacker was released while the victim herself was referred for arrest, which activists describe as evidence of a national hate policy. Comparable asymmetry recurs in custody: on 1 December 2025 a transgender prisoner was found dead in her cell at a women's prison near the capital, and rights groups demanded an independent investigation and changes to detention practices affecting transgender prisoners. Accounts from other trans prisoners and visiting lawyers state that four transgender inmates had been sent for psychiatric evaluation shortly before the death, that medical staff arrived after prolonged delay, that prosecutors and crime-scene investigators entered the prison only two days later, and that witness statements were not taken; an opposition MP raised the case in parliament on 12 December 2025.

Trans visitors who are detained are held in facilities organised by registered sex rather than gender identity, and the country's prisons subject LGBTI+ detainees to arbitrary body and strip searches, de facto isolation and restricted healthcare. Some prisoners refuse hospital transfers for fear of other male inmates. No policy or staff training exists to identify LGBTI+ needs, complaints are ineffective and can provoke further violence, and transfers are frequent. Event attendance carries its own exposure: monitoring of the 2025 capital-city Trans and LGBTI+ Pride Week found that violations of international human-rights law continuing since 2015 persisted through the year, with senior officials' discriminatory rhetoric deepening homophobia and transphobia.

Protection machinery is thin. The country has no comprehensive law prohibiting discrimination on sexual orientation or gender identity, and no direct discrimination protection for gender identity; a regional body's 2025 report found legal protection insufficient and out of line with its own standards, while noting official permissions granted to demonstrations promoting exclusion. If medication is needed during a stay, hormone replacement therapy is not covered by the government healthcare system, so trans visitors must obtain and pay for it privately.
blindTangential:
The province stands under the national framework; no province-specific divergence is documented. The national counts — 313 violations, 299 detention decisions, 6 right-to-life violations including 3 hate-motivated killings, 89 torture or ill-treatment violations, private-life violations rising from 16 to 67 including obstruction of trans people's hormone therapy, and 61 travel bans — are country-wide totals for 2025 as recorded by a national LGBTI+ rights organisation, not figures attributable to this province.

The obstruction of hormone therapy among the private-life violations bears directly on a trans visitor who needs medication during a stay, since hormone replacement therapy is not covered by the government healthcare system and must be obtained and paid for privately.
